practices.practice: MCP's built-in cursor-based pagination (an opaque `cursor`/`nextCursor` token pair, where the client MUST NOT assume a fixed page size or try to parse the cursor) applies ONLY to the four `*/list` discovery operations (`tools/list`, `resources/list`, `resources/templates/list`, `prompts/list`) — it is NOT a mechanism for paging the payload of an individual `tools/call` result.
practices.why: This is a scope boundary worth stating precisely: if a single tool call could return a huge result, the protocol gives the tool AUTHOR no free pagination primitive for that call — the burden to keep a single tools/call response small is entirely on the server/tool designer, using their own input parameters (limit/offset/filter args in their own inputSchema), not on the protocol.

practices.practice: Because there's no protocol-level cap on a single tool result, servers should 'implement some combination of pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation with sensible default parameter values for any tool responses that could use up lots of context.' Anthropic's own agent product, Claude Code, defaults to capping tool responses at 25,000 tokens and, on truncation, 'steer[s] agents with helpful instructions' rather than silently cutting output.
practices.why: A tool response that dumps an entire dataset costs context on every subsequent turn the model keeps that result in view; a numeric ceiling plus an actionable truncation message keeps the model informed that data was cut and how to ask for more, instead of silently degrading its view of the world.
practices.applies_to_logbook: `bin/ledger-server.mjs:53-54` does `JSON.stringify(result)` unconditionally for every tool, with no size cap, truncation, or pagination anywhere in the wire handler; tools like `get_resume_brief` or `reconcile` that could plausibly return large ledger content have no guard against an unbounded response reaching the model.

practices.practice: Prefer returning 'high signal information' over raw API fields the model doesn't need; avoid exposing 'low-level technical identifiers (for example: uuid, 256px_image_url, mime_type)' when a semantically meaningful label would do, and don't make a tool return data the caller can already derive or already has.
practices.why: Every token in a tool result is context the model must read and reason over on every subsequent turn; identifiers and redundant fields the model can't act on are pure cost with no benefit.

practices.practice: Servers MUST validate all tool inputs (a normative requirement in the spec's Security Considerations, independent of any business logic). The validation itself should happen against the JSON Schema declared in `inputSchema`, following the `$ref` resolution rules ($ref MUST NOT be auto-dereferenced across the network by default) so a client validating input/output against `inputSchema`/`outputSchema` doesn't become an SSRF (server-side request forgery) vector.
practices.why: This puts the authoritative validation boundary at the schema, not scattered ad hoc checks in handler code — and the $ref rule closes a specific attack where a malicious schema tries to make the validator fetch an attacker-controlled URL.
practices.applies_to_logbook: `src/tools/registry.mjs:36-41` compiles every tool's `inputSchema` with Ajv (a JSON Schema validator library) at startup and `callTool()` (`registry.mjs:57-67`) runs that compiled validator BEFORE invoking the tool handler, throwing a `ToolValidationError` with formatted per-field errors on failure — this directly satisfies the spec's 'servers MUST validate all tool inputs' requirement at the schema layer. logbook's schemas are all static, locally authored files (not fetched over the network), so the `$ref`-over-network SSRF concern doesn't currently apply to it as a schema source.

practices.practice: Communicate constraints to the model up front via unambiguous parameter naming (e.g. `user_id` rather than the generic `user`) and via the description text, rather than letting the model discover a constraint only by triggering a validation failure.
practices.why: A constraint stated in the schema/description is 'free' — the model reads it once per tool-list and can plan around it; a constraint discovered only via a failed call costs a full extra round trip (and burns the model's error budget) for something that was knowable in advance.
practices.applies_to_logbook: `src/tools/update-thread.mjs:130`'s description states several such constraints up front (e.g. that an empty array with no matching `replace_scopes` entry will be refused, and why), which is exactly this pattern — the constraint is documented in the tool description rather than left for the model to discover only by hitting the `assertNamesAScope` refusal at `update-thread.mjs:29-34`.

practices.practice: The spec's core trust principle for tools: 'Tools represent arbitrary code execution and must be treated with appropriate caution. In particular, descriptions of tool behavior such as annotations should be considered untrusted, unless obtained from a trusted server.' Hosts (the outer application) MUST obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool, and users should understand what a tool does before authorizing it.
practices.why: This is the spec's top-level framing for why tool metadata (names, descriptions, annotations) cannot be treated as inert documentation — an adversarial or compromised server can put anything it wants in a tool's description or annotations, and a client/host that blindly trusts that text is exposed to prompt injection through the tool's own definition, not just through its output.

practices.practice: Server-side security MUSTs from the spec: validate all tool inputs, implement proper access controls, rate-limit tool invocations, and 'sanitize tool outputs.' Client-side SHOULDs: prompt for user confirmation on sensitive operations, show tool inputs to the user before calling (to catch data-exfiltration attempts), validate tool RESULTS before passing them to the LLM, implement call timeouts, and log tool usage for audit.
practices.why: 'Sanitize tool outputs' and 'validate tool results before passing to LLM' are the spec's direct answer to the 'tool output is untrusted' concern: a tool's result content can itself carry adversarial instructions (indirect prompt injection) if it echoes untrusted external data (e.g. web page text, a file's contents) back to the model, so both the producing server and the consuming client carry a duty to treat that payload as data, not as instructions.
practices.applies_to_logbook: logbook runs entirely over `StdioServerTransport` (`bin/ledger-server.mjs:2,68`), i.e. local process-to-process communication with no network listener, so the dedicated MCP security-best-practices page's main content — confused-deputy OAuth-proxy attacks, token passthrough, SSRF against authorization-server metadata, localhost-redirect impersonation — is almost entirely about HTTP/OAuth transports and does not apply to logbook's current architecture. The residual concern that DOES apply is the general spec principle above: if any logbook tool result ever echoes back content that originated outside logbook's own control (e.g. arbitrary user-authored text stored in a ledger file that a different process could tamper with), that content re-enters the calling model's context as though it were logbook's own trusted output.

practices.practice: Composition keywords (`anyOf`/`oneOf`/`allOf`/`if-then-else`) and `$defs` in a JSON Schema 'can be expensive to validate'; implementations SHOULD bound schema depth, subschema count, or per-validation time to stop a malicious/pathological schema from becoming a denial-of-service vector against the validator itself.
practices.why: This is a security-adjacent addendum to the union-type schema-design guidance above: the same flexibility that makes union types useful (nested composition keywords) is also an attack surface if a schema-consuming implementation doesn't bound how much work it will do to validate one payload.
practices.applies_to_logbook: This bound matters for an implementation that validates THIRD-PARTY schemas at runtime; logbook only validates its own small set of statically authored `inputSchema`s (`src/tools/schemas.mjs` and per-tool files) with Ajv, so it is not acting as a general-purpose schema-consuming client exposed to adversarial schemas — the concern is not currently load-bearing for logbook, but would become relevant if logbook ever aggregated or proxied tools from other MCP servers.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Collapsing every failure mode — including 'unknown tool name' and malformed/schema-invalid requests — into a single generic try/catch that always returns `isError: true` inside an otherwise-successful `tools/call` result, instead of letting the transport layer return a JSON-RPC protocol error for the request-structure failures.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: The spec explicitly separates these two channels because they carry different information to the calling model: isError:true says 'you can probably fix this by retrying with different arguments,' while a protocol error says 'something is wrong with the request itself, and you're less likely to be able to fix it.' Flattening both into isError:true removes a signal the spec designed specifically to help the model decide whether retrying with adjusted arguments is even a sensible next step. logbook's `bin/ledger-server.mjs:49-61` does exactly this flattening (grounded read, not inference).

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Trusting a tool's `annotations` (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, etc.) — or any part of a tool's description — as ground truth for a security or consent decision, without regard to whether the server is a known/trusted one.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: Annotations and descriptions are self-reported by the server; a compromised or malicious server can label a destructive tool `readOnlyHint: true` to bypass a client's confirmation UI. The spec's warning is explicit and repeated in both the human-readable docs and the schema comments: 'Clients should never make tool use decisions based on ToolAnnotations received from untrusted servers.'

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Automatically dereferencing a `$ref` in an `inputSchema`/`outputSchema` that points to a remote network URI, without an allowlist, timeout, or size limit.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: This turns schema validation into a server-side request forgery (SSRF) primitive: an attacker-controlled schema can make the validating implementation fetch arbitrary internal URLs (e.g. cloud metadata endpoints) during what looks like ordinary input validation. The spec makes this a hard MUST NOT by default.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Wrapping every API endpoint in its own thin tool (one tool per CRUD operation: list_x, get_x, create_x, update_x, delete_x for every resource) instead of designing a smaller number of workflow-shaped tools.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: Anthropic's own engineering guidance states plainly that 'more tools don't always lead to better outcomes' and that overlapping/near-duplicate tools 'distract agents from pursuing efficient strategies' — the model has to spend reasoning budget just choosing among options that all resent themselves in every tool-list call.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Returning an unbounded tool result (e.g. an entire dataset, full file contents, or a raw API payload) with no truncation, pagination parameter, or size guard, on the assumption that MCP's protocol-level pagination will handle it.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: MCP's cursor-based pagination is scoped ONLY to the four discovery list operations (tools/list, resources/list, resources/templates/list, prompts/list); it does not apply to the payload of a `tools/call` result. A tool author who assumes otherwise ships a tool whose result size is genuinely unbounded, which can flood the model's context window on a single call.

open_questions: Should logbook adopt outputSchema/structuredContent for its tool results, given the pinned SDK (1.29.0) already implements both ends of that feature and logbook currently uses neither (confirmed by a repo-wide grep for these terms returning zero hits)? This would let a calling model rely on a declared shape instead of parsing an embedded JSON string inside a text content block.

Should bin/ledger-server.mjs's single catch-all in the CallToolRequestSchema handler (lines 49-61) be split so that 'unknown tool' and malformed-argument failures surface as JSON-RPC protocol errors (as the spec classifies them), while genuine business-logic failures (like update-thread.mjs's ToolError instances) remain isError:true tool results? Note src/tools/registry.mjs already internally distinguishes ToolError from ToolValidationError as separate JS error classes, so the raw material for this split already exists in the code - the flattening happens specifically at the ledger-server.mjs wire boundary.

Is there an intended or desired ceiling on individual tool-result size for logbook (comparable to Claude Code's 25,000-token default cap on tool responses), given bin/ledger-server.mjs:54 currently does an unbounded JSON.stringify(result) for every tool with no size guard?

Would adding tool annotations (readOnlyHint on get_resume_brief/read_decision, destructiveHint on archive_thread/reopen) provide meaningful value for logbook specifically, given it runs as a single trusted local stdio server rather than in a multi-server, multi-tenant client environment where the spec's consent-gating UI use case for annotations is most relevant?

Should the 14-tool set in src/tools/registry.mjs be reviewed against Anthropic's tool-consolidation guidance (e.g. whether transition_thread, update_thread, and amend_criteria could collapse into fewer workflow-shaped tools) - this would require reading each handler's actual behavior in more depth than this research pass covered before drawing a conclusion.

practices.practice: A plugin-bundled MCP server's tools are ALWAYS callable under the full scoped name mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool-name>; the bare mcp__<server-name>__<tool-name> form only exists when that same server is loaded directly (e.g. a project's own .mcp.json read outside the plugin-install mechanism). This applies uniformly to permission rules, a skill's allowed-tools list, a subagent's tools field, and hook matchers.
practices.why: Confirms the dual naming this project's SKILL.md files enumerate (mcp__ledger__* and mcp__plugin_logbook_ledger__*) is expected platform behavior, not a bug, and explains exactly which surfaces require the scoped name.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Matches skills/preflight/SKILL.md:4,13 and skills/debrief/SKILL.md:4,15 which list both mcp__ledger__<name> (server key from .mcp.json:3) and mcp__plugin_logbook_ledger__<name> (plugin name from plugin.json:2) for every tool.

practices.practice: Hook matchers targeting a plugin's bundled MCP server must also use the scoped name mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool>; a matcher written against the bare server key never fires for a plugin-bundled server.
practices.why: Independently corroborates the naming rule from a second, separate doc page (plugin component reference vs. the MCP reference page), which is the triangulation this repo's audit standard requires.
practices.applies_to_logbook: If this plugin ever adds hooks that watch ledger tool calls, they would need mcp__plugin_logbook_ledger__<tool> as the matcher, never mcp__ledger__<tool>.

practices.practice: There is no documented alias or single-glob shortcut that lets one allowed-tools/permission entry match both a bare server-scoped tool name and its plugin-scoped equivalent: allow-rule globs require a literal, wildcard-free server segment right after mcp__, and an unanchored glob like "mcp__*" is explicitly rejected with a warning in allow position (though it is valid in a deny rule).
practices.why: Directly answers whether the project could avoid listing both tool names in its skills' allowed-tools frontmatter: it cannot, given current Claude Code permission-glob semantics.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Explains why skills/preflight/SKILL.md and skills/debrief/SKILL.md must enumerate every tool twice rather than using one pattern like mcp__*ledger__* or mcp__*.

practices.practice: MCP tool schemas are deferred by default via Tool Search: only names and server instructions load at session start, full schemas load on demand, and Claude Code imposes no fixed per-server tool cap — the practical limit is the context window budget.
practices.why: Directly addresses how tool definitions consume context and what governs 'how many tools is too many.'
practices.applies_to_logbook: The ledger server's small tool set (8 tools) is unlikely to ever approach the token thresholds where this matters.

practices.practice: Claude Code truncates MCP tool descriptions and server instructions at 2KB each, so critical details should be placed near the start of both.
practices.why: Gives a concrete, documented ceiling for tool description length that server authors should design against.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Relevant if ledger tool descriptions in src/tools/index.mjs (not fully inspected in this pass) grow verbose; front-load the operative constraint in each description.

practices.practice: Tool definitions collectively consuming more than roughly 10K tokens are the point at which switching to Tool Search materially helps (one worked example showed an 85% token reduction).
practices.why: Gives a concrete numeric trigger for when tool-definition context cost becomes worth actively managing.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Useful as a future sizing check if the ledger server's tool count or description verbosity grows.

practices.practice: MCP tool output triggers a warning above 10,000 tokens and is hard-capped at 25,000 tokens by default in Claude Code (raisable via MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS); a server can self-declare a higher per-tool ceiling (up to 500,000 characters) via _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] in its tools/list response.
practices.why: Gives the concrete payload-size ceilings a tool-result-returning server must design within, and the escape hatch for legitimately large single-tool outputs.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Applies to any large ledger tool result (e.g. a full resume brief or a large decision drill-down); if either ever risks exceeding 25K tokens, annotate that specific tool rather than raising the global env var.

practices.practice: Bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality or create ambiguous decision points are called out as one of the most common failure modes: 'if a human engineer can't definitively say which tool should be used in a given situation, an AI agent can't be expected to do better.'
practices.why: This is the diagnostic test for whether a tool surface needs consolidation, more relevant than raw tool count.
practices.applies_to_logbook: The ledger's 8 tools each map to one distinct lifecycle step (reconcile, rebuild_index, get_resume_brief, read_decision, append_session_event, record_decision, amend_criteria, update_thread, transition_thread), which passes this test — no two tools compete for the same decision point.

practices.practice: Build a few thoughtful, consolidated tools rather than one tool per API endpoint; namespace tools by service/resource (e.g. asana_search, jira_search) to keep selection unambiguous as the tool library grows.
practices.why: Core guidance on tool-count and naming design that generalizes beyond any one MCP server.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Consistent with the ledger server already being registered under one namespaced key ('ledger'/'plugin_logbook_ledger') rather than exposing raw CRUD-per-endpoint tools.

practices.practice: A skill's allowed-tools frontmatter only pre-approves the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill (the grant clears on the next message) — it does not restrict which other tools remain callable; ongoing permission behavior for everything else is governed by the standard permission settings.
practices.why: Clarifies exactly what allowed-tools does and does not guarantee, relevant to any skill that lists MCP tools there for convenience.
practices.applies_to_logbook: skills/preflight/SKILL.md:4 and skills/debrief/SKILL.md:4 use allowed-tools purely to skip the permission prompt for ledger calls during that turn, not to sandbox the agent to only ledger tools.

practices.practice: Skill body content is loaded into context once and is not re-read on later turns; after auto-compaction, re-attached skills share a combined 25,000-token budget (first 5,000 tokens of each kept), so older-invoked skills can be dropped entirely. For behavior that must hold regardless of what remains in context, the docs redirect to hooks for deterministic enforcement rather than relying on skill prose.
practices.why: Establishes that a skill's prose is not a durable enforcement mechanism for operational constraints (caps, formats, ordering) across a long session, which bears directly on where such constraints should live.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Supports the plugin's own stated design in skills/preflight/SKILL.md:9 and skills/debrief/SKILL.md:9 ('the server owns... every rule') — constraints are enforced by the MCP server on every call, not by the skill's one-time prose.

practices.practice: MCP's own protocol distinguishes Protocol Errors (malformed requests, unknown tools — 'issues... models are less likely to be able to fix') from Tool Execution Errors (isError:true — 'actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters'); clients SHOULD surface the latter to the model to enable self-correction.
practices.why: Formalizes, at the protocol level, that hard operational constraints should be validated and communicated by the server via isError results, not assumed from skill instructions.
practices.applies_to_logbook: bin/ledger-server.mjs:51-60 wraps every thrown error into an isError:true tool_result, which is the structurally correct mechanism per this spec section; the quality of the individual error.message strings was not verified in this pass.

practices.practice: When a tool_result carries is_error:true with instructive text ('what went wrong + what to try next', e.g. 'Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds.'), Claude incorporates it and typically retries with corrected parameters, getting roughly 2-3 attempts before giving up and apologizing to the user; generic messages like 'failed' force it to guess.
practices.why: Directly answers what makes a tool error recoverable versus what triggers a retry loop, and gives a concrete, documented retry ceiling.
practices.applies_to_logbook: The ledger's error responses should include what constraint was violated and what value would be accepted, not just error.name/error.message passthrough, to land in the '2-3 retries succeed' outcome rather than the 'apologize and stop' outcome.

practices.practice: Claude Code's own MCP connection layer draws the same recoverable/unrecoverable line at the infrastructure level: transient errors (5xx, connection refused, timeout) are auto-retried up to 3 times with backoff; authentication and not-found errors are never auto-retried because they require a configuration change to resolve.
practices.why: Shows the recoverable-vs-not distinction is applied consistently by Claude Code itself, not just recommended for tool authors, reinforcing it as a real design axis.
practices.applies_to_logbook: General pattern-matching context only; no direct repo application identified.

practices.practice: Write tool descriptions with at least 3-4 sentences covering what the tool does, when to use it (and when not to), what each parameter means, and important caveats — described as 'by far the most important factor in tool performance.'
practices.why: Baseline, heavily emphasized guidance on tool-description quality that generalizes to any MCP tool author.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Applies to whatever descriptions src/tools/index.mjs supplies for each ledger tool; not directly inspected in this pass.

practices.practice: Design tool responses to return only high-signal information: semantic, stable identifiers rather than opaque internal references, and only the fields the model needs for its next step — bloated responses waste context and increase hallucination risk.
practices.why: Concrete guidance on 'returning the minimum useful result,' one of the six things this research was asked to check.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Relevant to how get_resume_brief and read_decision shape their returned payloads (not inspected in this pass).

practices.practice: Implement pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation with sensible default parameter values for any tool response that could grow large; optionally expose a response_format concise/detailed enum so the caller can trade off completeness against context cost.
practices.why: Direct guidance on payload-size management, one of the six things this research was asked to check.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Relevant if the ledger's session-log or decision-history reads ever grow unbounded; a paginate/filter/truncate default would keep get_resume_brief and read_decision within budget.

practices.practice: For multi-step state that must persist across tool calls, prefer an explicit create-then-reference 'handle' pattern (a creation tool returns an opaque ID; later calls pass it back) over folding all state into one call. Validate the caller's authorization against the handle on every call, keep handles opaque, document the handle's expected lifetime in the creation tool's own description, and return a clear execution error (not a silent no-op) when a handle is expired or unknown so the model can recover by creating a new one.
practices.why: This is MCP's own non-normative but explicit design guidance closest to 'confirming preconditions' and 'incremental vs all-or-nothing writes' for stateful agent-facing tools.
practices.applies_to_logbook: thread_id in the ledger tools (passed to append_session_event, record_decision, amend_criteria, update_thread, transition_thread per skills/debrief/SKILL.md) is exactly this handle pattern; whether expired/unknown thread_ids return a clear execution error was not verified in this pass.

practices.practice: MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint default false, destructiveHint default true, idempotentHint default false, openWorldHint default true) let a server hint at write/destructive/idempotent behavior, but the spec states these are hints only -- 'not guaranteed to faithfully describe tool behavior' -- and clients MUST treat them as untrusted unless the server itself is trusted; real safety gating (e.g. confirmation prompts) should sit in deterministic client-side controls, not solely rely on a server's self-reported annotation.
practices.why: Directly answers the idempotency-hint and precondition-confirmation part of the agent-facing API design question, and flags a security caveat about trusting those hints.
practices.applies_to_logbook: If the ledger server ever adds these annotations to its write tools, Claude Code would still treat them as advisory only from a first-party, already-trusted local server; they should not be relied on as the sole safety mechanism.

practices.practice: At-least-once delivery over a network is effectively unavoidable, so a write tool that can time out ambiguously (request may have succeeded even though the response was lost) needs an idempotency key so a retried call is a safe no-op rather than a duplicate write; the runtime/client, not the model, should generate the key by default (e.g. a hash of the canonical request content), and a reused key paired with a different request body should be rejected rather than silently merged.
practices.why: The most specific answer found anywhere (Anthropic or otherwise) to the idempotency-for-ambiguous-failures part of the question, but it is a single non-Anthropic vendor source, not corroborated elsewhere, so it is included at low confidence and clearly labeled.
practices.applies_to_logbook: The ledger's write tools (append_session_event, record_decision, amend_criteria, update_thread, transition_thread) are exactly the class of tool this pattern targets, since a git-based ledger write can plausibly be interrupted mid-operation; whether any idempotency mechanism exists in src/drivers was not inspected in this pass.

practices.practice: Tool results 'often carry content from sources outside your control: web pages, inbound email, user uploads, third-party APIs.' Treat that content as untrusted -- an attacker who can influence it may embed instructions trying to redirect Claude (indirect prompt injection) -- and keep such content inside tool_result blocks rather than system prompts or plain user text blocks.
practices.why: Directly and explicitly answers whether tool-result content is treated as untrusted data, with the precise architectural rule for where it must live in the message structure.
practices.applies_to_logbook: skills/preflight/SKILL.md:24 has the calling agent print the ledger's own briefing field verbatim; this is consistent with the untrusted-content rule only insofar as the ledger's own content is first-party/server-authored rather than externally sourced -- whether externally fetched or user-pasted text can enter decision/session-log bodies that are later rendered verbatim was not traced in this pass.

practices.practice: Claude Code implements the untrusted-tool-content boundary at the product level: web fetch runs in a separate context window 'to avoid injecting potentially malicious prompts,' Claude Code performs 'context-aware analysis' to detect harmful instructions, network-fetching Bash commands are never auto-approved, first-time MCP servers require trust verification, and the docs warn directly that 'servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection risk.'
practices.why: Shows the untrusted-content principle is enforced with concrete, product-level guardrails, not just stated as an abstract rule.
practices.applies_to_logbook: Ledger is a local, trusted first-party stdio server (no external fetch capability observed in bin/ledger-server.mjs), so the highest-risk guardrails here (isolated context windows for fetch, MCP trust verification) are less load-bearing for this specific server, but would matter if the plugin ever adds a tool that fetches external content.

practices.practice: MCP clients 'MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers' and 'SHOULD validate tool results before passing to LLM.'
practices.why: A third, independent primary source (the protocol spec itself) converging on the same untrusted-content boundary as the Claude API docs and Claude Code security docs.
practices.applies_to_logbook: General cross-corroboration; no direct repo application beyond reinforcing that the plugin's local server is a comparatively low-risk case for this specific rule.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Writing 'mcp__*' as an ALLOW rule (or an equivalent allowed-tools entry) expecting it to pre-approve every MCP tool across every server.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: Claude Code explicitly rejects unanchored allow-globs with a warning and grants no auto-approval at all, so the author gets silent no-op behavior instead of the intended broad allow (the same pattern works fine in a DENY rule, which is the trap).

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Relying on a skill's body text alone to enforce a hard operational constraint (a cap, a required format, a call ordering) for the rest of a long session.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: Skill content is injected once and is never re-read on later turns, and after auto-compaction only a shared 25,000-token budget (5,000 tokens per skill) is preserved -- older-invoked skills can be dropped entirely, silently un-enforcing anything that was stated only in their prose.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Returning generic tool-error text such as 'failed', a raw error code, or a stack trace instead of a specific, actionable message.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: Generic errors force the model to guess at a fix; both the Claude API docs and Anthropic's tool-writing guidance show that specific, actionable error text ('what went wrong + what to try next') is what lets Claude self-correct within its documented 2-3-retry window, and its absence increases the odds of the agent giving up or looping on the wrong fix.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Treating an MCP server's self-reported destructiveHint/idempotentHint annotations as a security guarantee that gates whether a destructive action needs confirmation.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: The MCP spec is explicit that annotations 'are not guaranteed to faithfully describe tool behavior' and clients 'MUST treat them as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server' -- a malicious or buggy server could mark a destructive write as idempotentHint:true and readOnlyHint:true to bypass a client's confirmation logic.

anti_patterns.anti_pattern: Building one narrow tool per API endpoint or operation instead of consolidating related operations into fewer tools with a clear, distinct purpose each.
anti_patterns.why_harmful: Anthropic's own engineering guidance names bloated tool sets with ambiguous decision points as one of the most common failure modes -- if a human engineer can't say definitively which tool applies, the agent can't either, and every extra tool definition also has a nonzero context cost even under deferred loading.

open_questions: Whether Claude Code has, or plans, any canonical/aliased tool-name registration so a skill would not need to enumerate both the bare (mcp__ledger__*) and plugin-scoped (mcp__plugin_logbook_ledger__*) MCP tool names -- no such mechanism is documented as of this research; 'list both' appears to be the only documented answer today.

Whether the ledger server's individual error.message strings (thrown inside src/tools/*, not read in this research pass) actually meet the 'specific and actionable' bar the Claude API docs recommend, or are generic passthroughs of the underlying JS error -- bin/ledger-server.mjs:51-60 shows only the wrapper, not the throw sites.

Whether the ledger's write tools (append_session_event, record_decision, amend_criteria, update_thread, transition_thread) implement any idempotency-key or retry-safety mechanism for a process/network interruption mid-write -- src/drivers and the deeper src/tools implementation were not read in this pass.

Whether any user-supplied or externally-fetched text can enter ledger decision/session-log bodies that skills/preflight/SKILL.md:24 later renders 'verbatim' to the user, which would put pressure on the untrusted-tool-content boundary documented for MCP generally -- would require tracing record_decision and append_session_event input handling, not done in this pass.

Anthropic has not published (as far as this research found) explicit idempotency-key guidance for MCP tool authors; the single source found for that exact pattern is a non-Anthropic vendor blog (Ledgenter), so it should be weighted as a lower-confidence, non-Anthropic best practice rather than platform-documented guidance if it informs any design decision.

clusters.cluster_name: Refusals the caller cannot act on: the error channel discards the detail that would make retry converge
clusters.root_cause: When the server says no, it throws away almost everything the caller would need to fix the call. Ajv knows exactly which property was unexpected, which branch of a union was meant, and which values are allowed, but src/schema/validators.mjs:10 keeps only `instancePath` and `message` and drops both `e.params` and `e.schemaPath`. So "must NOT have additional properties" never names the property, "must be equal to constant" never names the constant, and "must be equal to one of the allowed values" never lists them. A three-branch union (src/tools/schemas.mjs:72-109) compiled with allErrors:true (src/tools/registry.mjs:36) then reports all three branches' failures as one undifferentiated list, so a strike operation missing one field is told to add `text` and `kind` that a strike must not have. On top of that, bin/ledger-server.mjs:57 flattens every failure - bad argument, unknown tool, broken environment, corrupt stored record - into `{error: <JS class name>, message}`, so the model cannot tell which layer refused it or whether any retry could ever succeed. This is the known record_decision incident's mechanism generalized: an error that cannot distinguish 'the call did not parse' from 'the value was wrong'.
clusters.recommended_fix:
Give every refusal a machine-readable identity and make it name one hypothesis, not nine.

1. src/schema/validators.mjs - replace `formatValidationErrors` with a structured projection that reads `e.params`: emit the offending key for `additionalProperties` (`e.params.additionalProperty`), the constant for `const` (`e.params.allowedValue`), the members for `enum` (`e.params.allowedValues`), and for `pattern` the regex plus one conforming example string. Keep a rendered English line for humans, but derive it from the structured record rather than the reverse.

2. src/tools/schemas.mjs:72-109 - replace `criteriaAmendOperation`'s three-branch `oneOf` with a discriminated form: `properties.op: { enum: ['insert','rewrite','strike'] }` plus `allOf: [{ if: { properties: { op: { const: 'insert' } }, required: ['op'] }, then: <insert branch, additionalProperties:false> }, ...]`. Only the branch whose `op` actually matched contributes errors, so a missing `kind` on an insert yields exactly `operations[0] (op=insert): missing required property 'kind' (allowed: planned|detour)`. JSON Schema 2020-12 if/then/else is explicitly legal inside an MCP inputSchema.

3. Introduce one error envelope carried by all three existing error classes (ToolValidationError.errors at src/tools/registry.mjs:49, CapViolationError.fields at src/model/caps.mjs:24, SchemaValidationError.errors at src/schema/validators.mjs:19) and serialized once in bin/ledger-server.mjs:56-59 as `structuredContent` alongside the existing text: `{ code, layer: 'input-schema'|'handler-precondition'|'cap'|'stored-record'|'environment', tool, fields: [...], accepted_example, retryable: 'same-payload'|'different-payload'|'never' }`. Declare it as part of each tool's `outputSchema`. `layer: 'stored-record'` is what makes the readable-but-unwritable case recoverable: the model currently reads `/spine must have required property 'active_goal'` from a transition_thread call whose schema (src/tools/transition-thread.mjs:53-63) has no spine parameter, and has no way to learn the offending document is the record on disk.

4. Route `unknown tool` (src/tools/registry.mjs:59-61) and malformed CallToolRequest to a JSON-RPC protocol error instead of an isError result, per the spec's own example list. Keep everything a model can fix as isError:true.

5. Precondition errors enumerate rather than summarize: src/model/dod.mjs:8-10 returns the list of outstanding criterion ids and reports BOTH DoD failures at once instead of the first; src/tools/transition-thread.mjs:21,24 says "supplied but blank after trimming" when the value arrived rather than "is required"; src/tools/archive-thread.mjs:12-16 drops the hardcoded "a blocked thread must first go blocked -> paused" hint and branches on the actual cause the way src/tools/reopen.mjs:12-14 already does.
clusters.why_this_fix: MCP draws its error line at recoverability by the calling model: tool-execution errors exist so the model can 'self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters', and 'unknown tool' is named explicitly as a protocol error rather than an isError result - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools (Error Handling). Anthropic's tool-writing guidance requires error text that 'clearly communicate[s] specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks', and to show an example of correctly formatted input - https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents. The API tool-use docs put Claude's budget at roughly 2-3 retries before it gives up and apologizes, so a 689-char nine-clause error that points at the wrong fields consumes the entire budget on hypotheses that cannot work - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls. structuredContent/outputSchema is fully implemented in the pinned @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.29.0 and lets the detail be parsed instead of read as prose - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools (Structured Content).
rejected_alternatives: Set allErrors:false at src/tools/registry.mjs:36 - one-line fix, but with an undiscriminated oneOf ajv still reports the FIRST branch's failure, so a strike payload still gets an insert-branch complaint; it trades nine wrong clauses for one wrong clause and loses genuine multi-field feedback on the flat schemas where allErrors is actually useful.

Split amend_criteria into insert_criterion / rewrite_criterion / strike_criterion - removes the oneOf but breaks the documented atomic batch (src/tools/amend-criteria.mjs:110-113 applies operations in order and discards the whole call on failure), adds two tools against Anthropic's consolidation guidance, and leaves every other enum, const and additionalProperties error just as anonymous.

Document the union's branch requirements in amend_criteria's description instead - Claude Code truncates descriptions at 2KB and the description is read once at tools/list; the error is the only channel guaranteed present at the moment of failure, and the current error actively contradicts whatever the description says.

Return the raw ajv error array as JSON - dumps schemaPath and keyword noise the model must re-derive, gives no layer attribution or retryability signal, and the spec asks for actionable feedback rather than a validator dump.
clusters.risk: No on-disk format change and no accepted-payload change: the if/then/else rewrite of criteriaAmendOperation accepts exactly the same set of operations as the oneOf provided each branch keeps additionalProperties:false - if that is dropped during the rewrite, the schema silently widens and stops catching typo'd fields. Every test asserting exact error strings breaks and must be rewritten against the structured fields rather than the prose. Routing unknown-tool to a protocol error changes what a client sees for that one case; verify the host surfaces it rather than swallowing it. Enumerating outstanding criterion ids in the DoD message makes that message length proportional to criteria count - cap it.

clusters.cluster_name: No single definition of a valid record: the same value is accepted or refused depending on which door it came through
clusters.root_cause: There is no one place that says what a valid thread is. Constraints are written wherever someone happened to need them, in different vocabularies, and most exist in exactly one layer that only some of the writers pass through. src/model/caps.mjs:1-12 defines ten limits that appear nowhere in src/schema/thread.schema.mjs and are checked at exactly one call site (src/tools/update-thread.mjs:77) - and even there only against the fields THIS call submitted, never the merged spine that is actually written at update-thread.mjs:56-69,123. So a 400-char decision title written by record_decision (src/tools/record-decision.mjs:68-70, no cap check anywhere in that file) is stored fine and then refuses the identical value if update_thread ever restates it. The risk-sentence shape lives only in a handler regex (src/tools/spine-input.mjs:5) while the input schema advertises `minLength: 1` (src/tools/schemas.mjs:17) and the stored-record schema advertises the same (src/schema/thread.schema.mjs:17). Scope strings are pattern-checked (src/schema/patterns.mjs:24) but never checked against the criteria they must reference, so a risk filed under `c99` on a three-criterion thread is accepted and then invisible forever (src/model/selection.mjs:39-42, src/render/briefing.mjs:105). Thread slugs are `minLength: 1` at input (src/tools/open-thread.mjs:33) and at write (thread.schema.mjs:59) while decision slugs are pattern-enforced at the driver (src/drivers/local-driver.mjs:206). And the write path validates while the read path does not (local-driver.mjs:143-145 vs :147-148), so the v1 upcast (src/schema/upcast.mjs) can manufacture a record that reads and briefs perfectly and then hard-blocks every write.
clusters.recommended_fix:
Make src/schema/thread.schema.mjs the single normative definition of a valid record and derive every other layer from it.

1. Pull every constraint that currently lives only in a handler into the record schema: the ten SPINE_CAPS as maxLength/maxItems on spine properties (thread.schema.mjs:100-107); the risk-sentence `pattern` on riskItem.text (:17); `maxLength: 120` on decisionItem.title (:29); the 200-char criterion cap on completion_criteria items (:72); a slug `pattern` on threads matching the rule already enforced for decision slugs at local-driver.mjs:206 (:59); non-blank (trim-aware) rules for abandoned_reason and closure_statement (:94-95); `$` anchors on ISO_TIMESTAMP_PATTERN (src/schema/patterns.mjs:3-4); and one digit-width for DECISION_REF_PATTERN - pick `^[0-9]{4,}-[a-z0-9-]+$` to match the two layers that already tolerate growth (src/tools/read-decision.mjs:25, src/render/briefing.mjs:7) while local-driver.mjs:199 keeps padding to four.

2. Generate the tool input schemas from that record schema instead of hand-writing them in src/tools/schemas.mjs - a mechanical per-field projection, so `maxLength`, `pattern` and `enum` appear in tools/list and a schema-aware caller can truncate or reshape BEFORE sending. This is what removes the 'every cap is discoverable only by exceeding it' round trip at zero description cost. Keep the handler normalizers, but demote them to coercion only (bullet stripping, defaults) - never the sole home of a constraint.

3. Move the validation choke point from the submitted patch to the merged record. Delete `assertSpineCaps(submitted)` at update-thread.mjs:77 and make `writeThread` (local-driver.mjs:147-153) the one place that validates the whole record, so record_decision (record-decision.mjs:76), amend_criteria (:115) and transition_thread (:39) inherit caps automatically.

4. Add a new src/model/invariants.mjs holding the referential checks JSON Schema cannot express, also called from writeThread: every risk/decision scope is `thread`, `legacy`, or an EXISTING criterion id; every key_decisions[].ref resolves to a decision file and its title matches the file's `# {nnnn}. {title}` heading (src/tools/record-decision.mjs:23) rather than being free text; key_decisions unique by ref; detour non-nesting (today enforced only in one handler at amend-criteria.mjs:50-56 and bypassable at creation via criteriaCreateItem); slug uniqueness across threads.

5. Validate on read, not only on write. `readThread` validates after upcast and returns `{thread, schema_health}`; `listThreads` (local-driver.mjs:155-164) upcasts identically instead of returning raw v1 records to the index builder (src/index/rebuild-index.mjs:41-44) and the briefing (src/tools/get-resume-brief.mjs:19-27). Add a property test that every v1 fixture, upcast, validates against the v2 (soon v3) schema, so a migration that produces an invalid record fails in CI rather than in a user's session.

6. Fix the two record_decision shape traps at the schema: collapse the `options` union (record-decision.mjs:93-98) to a single `array<string>` with `minItems: 1` and item `minLength: 1` - or, if the string form is kept, run BOTH branches through the same normalizer instead of short-circuiting the array branch at :9; give `context` and `outcome` `minLength`. Make `kind` consistently optional-with-default across criteriaCreateItem (schemas.mjs:48-56) and the amend insert branch (:79). Give open_thread/create_successor an explicit slug fallback so a non-Latin title (src/model/thread.mjs:57-59) is not a hard failure.
clusters.why_this_fix: MCP makes input validation a server MUST and locates the authoritative boundary at the declared schema rather than in ad-hoc handler checks - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools (Security Considerations). Anthropic's tool-writing guidance says to communicate constraints up front through parameter naming and the schema 'rather than letting the model discover a constraint only by triggering a validation failure', because a schema-stated constraint is free (read once per tools/list) while a discovered one costs a full round trip - https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents. Claude Code truncates tool descriptions at 2KB, which is why ten numeric caps belong in maxLength keywords and not in update_thread's already-831-char description - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.
rejected_alternatives: Just add assertSpineCaps to record_decision as well - closes one named gap and preserves the structure that produced all of them; the next tool that touches the spine reintroduces it, and it does nothing about the read/write asymmetry or the referential (scope, ref, title) gaps that are the actually-destructive ones.

Put the constraints in the input schemas only and leave thread.schema.mjs permissive - keeps behavior entry-point-dependent (the upcast and any future writer still bypass it) and keeps the ledger able to hold records its own tools would refuse, which is precisely the readable-but-unwritable trap.

Enforce caps by truncating instead of throwing, matching what the user's global continuity rule already claims happens - silently loses the tail of the only copy of active_goal/next_step (src/render/briefing.mjs:9-12,51,89 already show what silent truncation looks like: a '...' that reads as stylistic), and reverses the decision recorded at docs/specs/2026-08-02-preflight-briefing-redesign.md:151.

Leave the on-disk schema alone and ship a separate `ledger lint` command - avoids the migration entirely, but the write path stays able to accept invalid records, so the linter permanently reports drift it has no power to prevent.
clusters.risk: This is the cluster that BREAKS ON-DISK COMPATIBILITY. Tightening thread.schema.mjs means already-committed ledgers can hold records the new schema rejects: over-cap active_goal/next_step written before caps existed or carried through update_thread's patch-only check; over-cap decision titles written by record_decision; risks with no spaced em dash - including EVERY v1-upcast risk, since src/schema/upcast.mjs:44 wraps a bare string with no shape check; `legacy`-scoped decisions (upcast.mjs:53-59) that the writable-scope pattern forbids; empty-string v1 risks and out_of_scope entries that already fail v2's minLength; duplicate slugs; and scopes naming criteria that never existed. Required migration: bump THREAD_SCHEMA_VERSION to 3 and ship `ledger-cli migrate --check | --repair` that (a) reports every violation as file+field+value, (b) repairs mechanically only where the repair is information-preserving - demote over-cap scalars into a session-log entry and leave a pointer, remap `legacy` scope to `thread`, suffix duplicate slugs with the ULID's last 6 chars, rewrite a shapeless risk as `<text> - migrated from v1, rationale not recorded` - and (c) refuses ambiguous cases and lists them for a human. Keep the v2 reader for one release so an unmigrated ledger degrades rather than erroring at session start. Second risk: validating on read turns a corrupt record from 'briefs fine, blocks writes' into 'fails at read', which is more honest but louder - it must surface as a repairable schema_health warning, not a thrown error, or a single bad file takes out the whole roster.

clusters.cluster_name: Writes have no transaction boundary, no idempotency key, and no concurrency check, so failures and retries leave permanent junk
clusters.root_cause: Every mutating tool performs several separate durable writes - a decision markdown file, then the thread JSON, then the active-thread pointer, then a session event, then a git commit - with no ordering rule, no rollback, no dedup key, and no check that the record on disk is still the one the handler read. record_decision writes the file at src/tools/record-decision.mjs:66 and only validates the thread ten lines later at :76, where src/drivers/local-driver.mjs:148 is the first and only validation; a throw there leaves an orphan numbered decision on disk that no tool can remove, and because src/drivers/local-driver.mjs:189-199 derives the next number by scanning the directory, that orphan permanently advances the counter so the retry mints a DIFFERENT number. The same write-then-side-effect ordering exists at transition-thread.mjs:39 before :40-45, open-thread.mjs:18 before :19, archive-thread.mjs:24 before :28 and reopen.mjs:28 before :29. Nothing anywhere compares against what is on disk, so two concurrent read-modify-write calls silently lose one. The model is told the call failed - the single most retry-inducing signal there is - and its retry creates a second permanent record.
clusters.recommended_fix:
Give every mutation a validate-first ordering, a stale-record check, and a retry-safe key.

1. Validate-then-write, everywhere. In src/tools/record-decision.mjs, build the candidate thread and run the full record validation (the single choke point from the schema-coherence cluster) BEFORE `driver.writeDecision` at :66; the decision file becomes the LAST durable write. Apply the same reordering wherever a throwing side effect follows a durable write: transition-thread.mjs:39 vs :40-45 (writeActiveThread/clearActiveThread throw when CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA is unset for a non-git project, src/util/active-thread.mjs:26-27), open-thread.mjs:18 vs :19, archive-thread.mjs:24 vs :28, reopen.mjs:28 vs :29-30. Any side effect that cannot be moved before the record write is made non-throwing and reported in the result instead.

2. Optimistic concurrency. Every write result carries `updated_at` (or a monotonic `revision`); every mutating tool accepts an optional `if_unmodified_since`. `writeThread` (local-driver.mjs:147-153) re-reads the record and refuses on mismatch with `code: 'stale-record'` plus the current value, telling the model to re-read and re-apply. Without this, two record_decision calls issued concurrently both report success while one spine entry is silently clobbered - the MCP SDK dispatches requests concurrently, so this is reachable in normal operation, not just under adversarial load.

3. Idempotency key. Every mutating tool accepts an optional `idempotency_key`; the driver keeps `index/idempotency.json` mapping key to `{tool, request_hash, result}`. A repeat with the same key returns the STORED result (a safe no-op); a repeat with the same key and a different body is refused rather than merged. For record_decision, default the key server-side to a hash of (thread_id, slug, title) so even a naive retry that supplies no key cannot mint 0009 and 0010 for the same decision - and delete the dead `some(d => d.ref === ref)` guard at record-decision.mjs:68, which can never fire because :67 builds `ref` from a number that is always max+1.

4. Replace the naked `recovery_degraded` boolean (src/tools/shared.mjs:19-23, attached to every write return with its meaning documented in none of the 14 descriptions) with a declared `durability: { written: true, committed: false, reason: '<git failure>', action: 'do not retry - the record is on disk; tell the user the ledger is uncommitted' }`, sourced from the swallow at local-driver.mjs:298-300 and declared in each tool's outputSchema. The current boolean costs tokens on every call, conveys nothing actionable, and the one recovery it invites - retry - is precisely the wrong answer given (3).

5. Add `readOnlyHint`/`destructiveHint`/`idempotentHint` annotations to all 14 tools in src/tools/registry.mjs:19-34 - currently absent, so every tool defaults to the most dangerous profile in any host that reads them. Advisory only; the enforcement is (1)-(3).
clusters.why_this_fix: At-least-once delivery makes ambiguous write failures unavoidable, and the specific documented remedy is an idempotency key generated by the runtime rather than by the model, with a same-key-different-body rejection instead of a silent merge - https://ledgenter.com/blog/agent-writes-need-idempotency-keys (single non-Anthropic source, low confidence, but it is the only guidance found at this specificity and it matches the reproduced duplicate-decision behavior exactly). MCP's own create-then-reference handle guidance requires that an unknown or expired reference produce a clear execution error rather than a silent no-op so the model can recover - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools. Annotations are hints the spec says MUST NOT be trusted as a safety mechanism, which is why they are the last item here and not the fix - https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-03-16-tool-annotations/.
rejected_alternatives: Wrap each handler in a try/catch that unlinks whatever it already wrote - compensating deletes are themselves writes that can fail, and the failure window that actually matters (process death, or a transport loss AFTER the write landed) never runs the catch block at all; it would fix only the narrow validation-throw case while leaving the ambiguous-transport case, which is the one that generated the reproduced duplicates.

Document in each description that writes are not retry-safe - shifts the burden to a caller that by construction has no evidence whether the first call landed; the defining property of the ambiguous-failure case is that the model cannot distinguish 'never arrived' from 'succeeded, response lost'.

Take a per-thread file lock - serializes concurrent read-modify-write correctly but does nothing for retry-after-ambiguous-failure, and it cannot be held across the git backend's worktree teardown (src/drivers/git-ref-driver.mjs:354-359).

Make each tool exactly one git commit and roll back with git reset - index/ is gitignored (src/drivers/git-ref-driver.mjs:29) so not all state is inside the commit, and the local backend explicitly tolerates a degraded, uncommitted write (local-driver.mjs:298-300), so the commit cannot serve as the transaction boundary.
clusters.risk: Renaming `recovery_degraded` to `durability` changes an existing return shape on eight tools - ship both for one release with the boolean marked deprecated in the outputSchema. No on-disk record format change, but a NEW on-disk artifact (index/idempotency.json) needs a retention policy or it grows without bound; put it under index/, which is already gitignored on the git backend, and accept that the git backend therefore gets no cross-process idempotency until index/ persistence is fixed separately. Reordering record_decision so the file is written last changes the observable failure mode from 'orphan file, error returned' to 'no file, error returned' - correct, but any existing repair tooling or test that expects the orphan breaks. The optimistic-concurrency check adds one extra read per write; on the git backend that read is cheap relative to the commit. Existing ledgers already containing orphan decision files and duplicate threads are not fixed by this cluster - the migration/repair tool from the schema-coherence cluster must also detect decision files referenced by no thread spine and duplicate-slug threads, and offer to renumber or archive them.

clusters.cluster_name: Silent success: a write does something other than what was asked and the return value cannot reveal it
clusters.root_cause: A call can destroy data, do nothing, or mutate a record it should not touch, and still return success - because the result never says what actually changed, only what the record now is. Three shapes of the same cause. (a) Omission means delete: `spine.out_of_scope` is replaced wholesale by a plain spread at src/tools/update-thread.mjs:58, while its two sibling arrays are merged by scope at :59-68 and the description at :130 spends its longest passage teaching that merge rule - so a model that generalizes correctly wipes every prior session's entries. Naming a scope in `replace_scopes` with nothing submitted for it likewise deletes that scope's contents (:18-27), which is how debrief step 5 destroys the decision links step 3 created minutes earlier. (b) Naming something that does not exist is a no-op rather than an error: a scope holding nothing is silently accepted (:18-27), and `legacy` - which the v1 upcast stamps onto every migrated decision (src/schema/upcast.mjs:53-59) and which storage permits (src/schema/patterns.mjs:22) - cannot be named at all because every input schema forbids it (:24), so the only entries that need retiring are the only ones that cannot be. (c) A documented pure read mutates: get_resume_brief consumes the drift snapshot (src/tools/get-resume-brief.mjs:28 into src/drift/snapshot.mjs:90-92, a filter-and-write-back) and arms a Stop-hook print obligation (:30-34), while its own description at :40 says 'The rendered string is the only payload.'
clusters.recommended_fix:
Make every mutation report its effect, and make destruction require explicit intent.

1. Declare an `outputSchema` on all 14 tools and return `structuredContent`. For mutating tools the payload is an EFFECT REPORT, not the record: `{ thread_id, status, updated_at, changed: { <field>: { added: [...], removed: [...], carried: <n>, replaced_scopes: [...] } }, warnings: [...], durability: {...} }`. Removals are first-class visible entries, so a caller that names `c3` in replace_scopes.key_decisions sees `removed: ['0007-x','0008-y']` and can tell it just deleted what it recorded minutes ago. This single change converts every defect in this cluster from silent to observable, which is why it leads.

2. Make deletion require intent. Add `out_of_scope` to SCOPED_SPINE_FIELDS (src/tools/spine-input.mjs:10) and to replaceScopesInput (src/tools/schemas.mjs:39-46) so it merges like its siblings and a submitted array can never silently drop another session's entries. Naming a scope that holds nothing becomes a refusal naming the scopes that DO hold items, not a no-op, unless the call passes `allow_empty_scope: true`. Make `legacy` namable in replace_scopes (it is already a legal stored scope) so the one class of entry that can never be retired becomes retirable - and delete the unreachable explanatory throw at spine-input.mjs:12-19, which ajv preempts in every caller-supplied case.

3. Split get_resume_brief's read from its side effects. The render becomes idempotent and repeatable. Drift is REPORTED, not consumed: move the destructive half of src/drift/snapshot.mjs:86-92 into a separate explicit `acknowledge_drift(thread_id, entry_ids)` tool, so re-rendering a briefing can never lose a deleted-or-diverged-branch report. The verbatim pledge is armed by an explicit `pledge: true` parameter defaulting to false, so re-rendering does not re-arm an obligation the caller did not request. Update the description to state both remaining side effects, and set `readOnlyHint: false` honestly.

4. Close the guard asymmetries so the model can form one rule about what terminal means. `record_decision` gets the `isTerminal` refusal both its sibling spine writers already have (mirror src/tools/update-thread.mjs:109-111 at record-decision.mjs:51); so do `bind_branch` (src/tools/bind-branch.mjs:8-14) and `append_session_event`. `bind_branch` stops writing the active-thread pointer for a non-active thread at :14 - or, equivalently, the pointer clears at transition-thread.mjs:42 and archive-thread.mjs:25 stop gating on `thread.status === 'active'`, so a bound-then-paused thread can still be released and the Stop hook is not deadlocked. `transition_thread` preserves the blocker on blocked -> paused rather than nulling it at :30 (write it into the session event at :45 at minimum), and REFUSES a `closure_statement` supplied for a non-done target instead of silently dropping it at :32.

5. Collapse `archive_thread` and `reopen` into `transition_thread`, or make them thin aliases that call the identical code path. Three tools covering overlapping regions of one five-state FSM with three different validation rules is what let a whitespace-only abandonment reason through src/tools/archive-thread.mjs:42 that src/tools/transition-thread.mjs:23-25 refuses. Fix archive_thread's description claim at :35 that it 'clears the active pointer' when :25 only sometimes does.

6. Read-side honesty, since these effects are read back through the briefing: the DECIDED ON THIS STEP block (src/render/briefing.mjs:119-127) separates thread-scoped standing decisions under their own subheading exactly as the risks block already does at :107-114, so a deliberately promoted decision is not misfiled as decided-this-step; the NOT SHOWN block (:150-156) names the hidden scopes rather than counting them; and `record_decision`'s effect report states the scope it landed in and whether that scope will still be visible after the current criterion closes.
clusters.why_this_fix: Anthropic's guidance is that a tool result should carry the high-signal information the model needs for its NEXT step - for a mutation that is what changed, not a re-dump of state the caller already sent - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools. outputSchema/structuredContent is the spec-sanctioned way to return typed, parseable results and is fully implemented in the pinned SDK 1.29.0, yet a repo-wide grep finds zero uses - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools (Structured Content). MCP's handle guidance is explicit that an unknown or expired reference must produce a clear execution error rather than a silent no-op, which is exactly what naming an empty or nonexistent scope violates today - same page. Tool annotations let the host mark get_resume_brief honestly as non-read-only, though the spec is equally clear they are hints and never the enforcement - https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-03-16-tool-annotations/.
rejected_alternatives: Add the out_of_scope replace-all rule to update_thread's description - the description already devotes roughly 700 of its 831 characters to teaching the OPPOSITE rule for the sibling arrays (src/tools/update-thread.mjs:130), so the model that reasons correctly from the documented rule is precisely the one that loses data; the asymmetry is the defect, and documenting an asymmetry that has no reason to exist just moves the trap.

Make get_resume_brief non-destructive by having the Stop hook clear the drift instead - the hook path is already structurally dead on the git backend, because index/ is gitignored and the worktree is wiped on every context build (src/drivers/git-ref-driver.mjs:29,354-359), so this relocates the clear to somewhere it provably never runs.

Keep returning the full thread and let the model diff it against what it sent - that is today's behavior; a measured ~6.3 KB / ~1,570-token echo of which ~83% is untouched content invites reasoning from a stale blob, and the removal the model most needs to notice is invisible precisely because it is an absence.

Deprecate replace_scopes and require every call to resubmit the complete array - makes each write an all-or-nothing restatement of state the model may no longer hold (and, per the debrief-payload finding, at the moment its context is most exhausted), which is the exact failure the scoped design exists to prevent.
clusters.risk: No on-disk format change, but two live contract changes. First, mutating tools stop returning `thread`, which breaks any caller or test reading `result.thread` - ship it behind `include_thread: true` for one release. Second, out_of_scope changes from replace-all to scoped-merge: existing callers that submitted the full list every time now get merge-with-carry, which is safe (nothing is lost) but means a caller that intended a deletion silently stops deleting - the effect report makes that visible, and `replace_scopes.out_of_scope` is the explicit path. Note that data ALREADY destroyed by a prior wholesale replace is not recoverable from the ledger; only from git history of the thread JSON, and the migration tool should say so rather than implying repair. Adding a terminal guard to record_decision and bind_branch will start refusing calls that previously succeeded - correct, but any workflow relying on post-closure decision capture must move to create_successor. Splitting drift acknowledgement into its own tool means an existing caller that never calls it will accumulate drift entries; make acknowledge_drift idempotent and have the briefing show the entry count so the growth is visible.

clusters.cluster_name: The server can write state but cannot show it, so identifiers survive only in the model's head and every write compensates by echoing the whole record
clusters.root_cause: Twelve of the fourteen tools require a ULID that no tool returns unless you just created the thread. The one tool the preflight skill is told to call for the roster computes the full roster (src/index/rebuild-index.mjs:45-54) and the slug-to-id map (:64), writes both to files, and then returns six integers (:69-76, surfaced at src/tools/rebuild-index.mjs:4-7) - which reads to the model like a successful roster fetch that yields nothing usable. There is no enumeration tool and no slug resolution, so the identifier the entire write side is keyed on reaches the model exactly once, as prose in a SessionStart injection. Server-assigned values are likewise strandable: record_decision computes the canonical `ref` at src/tools/record-decision.mjs:67, uses it at :68-70, and discards it from the return at :78 in favor of an absolute filesystem path an MCP caller cannot act on; amend_criteria assigns a detour id that does not match its insert position (src/tools/amend-criteria.mjs:60-66 with src/model/criteria.mjs:3-11) and surfaces it only inside the full-thread echo. And because there is no read tool, every write echoes the entire record (update-thread.mjs:125 and six siblings), measured at ~1,570 tokens for a 43-character edit.
clusters.recommended_fix:
Add the missing read surface, and shrink the write returns now that they are no longer the only source of state.

1. New `list_threads` tool (src/tools/list-threads.mjs), no required arguments, optional `{ status?, slug?, limit = 20 }`, declared outputSchema. It returns the roster src/index/rebuild-index.mjs:45-54 already builds - `{id, slug, title, status, next_step, done, total, detours_open}` - and resolves a slug to a ULID from the by-slug map at :64. This is what preflight calls instead of `rebuild_index`, and it makes the documented `/preflight <slug>` path (skills/preflight/SKILL.md:18) resolvable in-protocol against an index the server already maintains for exactly this purpose.

2. New `get_thread` tool with `view: 'spine' | 'criteria' | 'full'` (default `spine`). This is how a model re-reads criterion ids, decision refs, and which criteria are still outstanding without performing a write - the thing that currently makes a failed `transition_thread(to:'done')` unrecoverable. Either give `rebuild_index` the roster in its return too, or drop it from both skills, since its effect is already guaranteed by `commitAndReindex` on every mutating call (src/tools/shared.mjs:19-23).

3. Mutating tools stop returning `thread`. They return the effect report from the silent-success cluster plus exactly the identifiers the next call needs: `record_decision` returns `ref` (already computed at record-decision.mjs:67) and drops the unusable absolute `path`; `amend_criteria` returns the ids of criteria it inserted, rewrote or struck, so a step-4 detour insert hands step 5 the id it must toggle; `transition_thread` returns status plus the pointer state. Across the five-plus writes a debrief performs, this is a 5-8k-token reduction at the point in the session where context is scarcest.

4. Widen `create_successor` to the same field set `open_thread` accepts - `slug`, `vcs_ref`, `external_refs` (src/tools/create-successor.mjs:34-38 vs src/tools/open-thread.mjs:31-39) - since none of the three can be set by any later tool, so today a successor is permanently without its ticket link and the only workaround (call open_thread instead) discards the predecessor linkage the tool exists to create.

5. Read-side legibility: make `whyBlock` and `nextStepBlock` (src/render/briefing.mjs:50-52, 88-90) conditional like `lastSessionBlock` at :83-86 - which is what the spec at docs/specs/2026-08-02-preflight-briefing-redesign.md:186-187 already requires - and emit an explicit 'no spine recorded: the previous session did not complete a hand-off' line so a never-debriefed thread is distinguishable from one whose debrief failed. Align the roster's 120-char next_step truncation (hooks/lib/roster.mjs:2) with the 500-char cap (src/model/caps.mjs:3) in one direction or the other, since the roster is the surface used to CHOOSE a thread.

6. Bound the wire payload: bin/ledger-server.mjs:53-54 stringifies every result with no size guard. Add a ceiling with an actionable truncation notice, and for the one tool that legitimately returns a large string (get_resume_brief) declare `_meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"]` rather than raising a global environment variable.
clusters.why_this_fix: MCP's own guidance for multi-step state is create-then-reference: a creation tool returns an opaque id and later calls pass it back - which presupposes the id is actually RETURNED, and that an unknown handle yields a recoverable error rather than a dead end - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools. Anthropic's tool guidance says to return only the high-signal information needed for the next step and not data the caller already holds, and explicitly calls out returning unusable low-level identifiers - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools and https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents. MCP's cursor pagination is scoped strictly to the four */list discovery operations and does NOT apply to a tools/call payload, so keeping a single result small is entirely the tool author's job - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/utilities/pagination; Claude Code warns above 10k tokens of MCP output and hard-caps at 25k - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp. Going from 14 to 16 tools stays far inside the ~10k-token definition budget where tool count starts to cost - https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use - and both new tools pass the 'a human engineer can say definitively which tool applies' test - https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents.
rejected_alternatives: Have rebuild_index return the roster it already computes - a one-line change and strictly better than today, but it leaves a write-shaped tool (it rewrites four index files on every call) as the sole read path, so the model must mutate in order to look, and it still gives no per-thread projection for criterion ids, decision refs, or outstanding criteria.

Re-inject the roster on more UserPromptSubmit triggers by widening the RESUME_INTENT regex at hooks/lib/user-prompt-submit.mjs:3 - keeps the identifier out-of-band, so it still cannot survive compaction, a subagent dispatch, or a debrief many turns after session start; it also makes the server's usability depend on hook prose the server does not control, and the same class of gap reappears for criterion ids and decision refs which no hook injects at all.

Keep echoing the full thread so the model always holds current state - measured at ~6.3 KB per write with ~97% not-new information, repeated five-plus times in one wrap-up, forcing the model to reconcile near-identical blobs and inviting it to reason from a stale echo.

Expose the ledger as MCP resources instead of tools - resources are client-fetched and are not guaranteed to be in the model's context at the moment of a write; the identifier is needed inside a tool-call loop, which is precisely the case tools serve and resources do not.
clusters.risk: No on-disk change. Two contract changes: mutating tools stop returning the full record (breaks anything reading `result.thread`; gate behind `include_thread: true` for one release and remove after), and dropping `path` from record_decision's return removes a field nothing can legitimately use over MCP but which a local script might. `list_threads` exposes thread titles and next_step text that today only reach the model through the SessionStart roster - no new trust boundary, since it is the same first-party content, but it is a new place unbounded user-authored text enters context, so apply the same truncation the roster does and keep it inside the tool-result block. If list_threads reads the persisted index rather than recomputing, it inherits the finding that index/ is empty in a freshly started process on the git backend (src/drivers/git-ref-driver.mjs:29,354-359) - it must call rebuildIndex in-process or read threads directly, or it will return an empty roster on the backend where it matters most.

clusters.cluster_name: The operating manual and the machine disagree, and the manual is the layer that does not survive the session
clusters.root_cause: The rules a caller must follow are split across three layers that contradict each other and the code. An always-loaded user-global rule file describes a different system (different skill names, a markdown file layout the server never reads, caps measured in lines, an automatic hand-off transition, criteria fixed at creation, and cap violations that demote rather than throw - the exact opposite of src/model/caps.mjs:119-124). Two deliberately thin skill files carry the operational procedure, and a test at test/unit/skills/skill-invariants.mjs:12 explicitly forbids either of them from containing the string 'active -> paused' - the single precondition the documented flow needs. Tool descriptions omit the rest: transition_thread's 95 characters (src/tools/transition-thread.mjs:52) never mention that closure_statement is required for done. The result is that the default documented flow does not execute: preflight exposes no write tool (skills/preflight/SKILL.md:4, asserted at test/unit/skills/preflight.test.mjs:44-49) so nothing ever makes a thread active; debrief step 6 asks for paused (skills/debrief/SKILL.md:34-35); paused -> paused is illegal (src/model/fsm.mjs:13, refused at transition-thread.mjs:18); and the Stop gate meant to force a hand-off fires only on an active-thread pointer that the documented flow never sets (hooks/lib/stop.mjs:101-104). Skill prose is loaded once and can be dropped entirely on compaction, so it is the worst possible home for any of this.
clusters.recommended_fix:
Make the documented flow executable in the SERVER, then reduce the skills to routing.

1. Close the FSM gap so the resume path exists. Add an explicit resume: either `get_resume_brief` gains `resume: true` performing paused -> active and setting the pointer, or a dedicated `resume_thread` tool does it - and add that tool to preflight's allowed-tools (skills/preflight/SKILL.md:4) and to the preflight invariant test.
